topic: Intermediary buffering defeating an event stream
stem: A government benefits portal added streaming to its eligibility explainer so applicants see text appear rather than staring at a spinner. Against the origin service, tokens arrive incrementally exactly as expected. Through the public URL, applicants still see nothing for eight seconds and then the whole explanation at once. The path from the browser to the origin runs through a CDN and a reverse proxy.

options.text: Shorten the explanation so the intermediary's buffer fills and flushes more often during generation.
Configure the CDN and reverse proxy to pass event streams through unbuffered, and verify from the browser.
Move the explainer to WebSockets, since HTTP intermediaries cannot forward an incrementally generated response.
Ask the model for shorter sentences so the origin emits smaller, more frequent events over the stream.

explanation.correct: The stem isolates the fault precisely: incremental at the origin, all-at-once through the public path, so something between them is accumulating the body before forwarding it. Response buffering is default behaviour in most proxies and CDNs because it is the right thing for ordinary responses, and it silently converts a stream back into a single delivery. The fix is a path configuration change, and the verification must be done from the browser, because testing against the origin is exactly what let this reach production.

distractors.A: Buffer behaviour is not driven by the size of the payload; a shorter explanation arrives all at once too, just sooner. This also degrades the product to work around a configuration defect.
distractors.C: Event streams over HTTP forward perfectly well through correctly configured intermediaries. Rewriting the transport is a large change that leaves the same misconfigured hops in the path for every other streaming endpoint.
distractors.D: Event frequency at the origin is already fine, as the origin-side test shows. Changing generation style cannot influence what an intermediary does with the bytes it receives.

explanation.concept: Streaming is an end-to-end property. Every hop between the model and the user — load balancer, reverse proxy, CDN, API gateway, application framework — must forward incrementally, and most of them buffer by default. Always validate streaming from the real client through the real path, never from the origin.
explanation.tip: 'Works at the origin, not through the edge' localises the fault to the path. When a stem carefully lists the intermediaries, they are the answer, not the model call.

topic: Work whose output exceeds the model's output ceiling
stem: An education publisher generates full curriculum guides — thirty to forty pages of structured material — from a syllabus in a single call. The team has already set the output allowance to the highest value the model accepts, and the longer syllabi still return with a `max_tokens` stop reason. They have tried three models in the same family and see the same behaviour on the same inputs.

options.text: Enable streaming, which lifts the per-response output limit because tokens are delivered as produced, not in one body.
Retry the truncated requests, since generated length varies between samples and an attempt will eventually fit.
Decompose the guide into sections generated by separate calls against a shared plan, and assemble the results client-side.
Set the output allowance above the model's ceiling and log the resulting validation error as a warning to ignore.

explanation.correct: The team has already exhausted the only parameter available: the allowance is at the model's ceiling, and the same behaviour appears across models, so this is a structural limit rather than a configuration mistake. A document that legitimately exceeds what one response can hold has to be produced in parts. Generating a plan first and then each section against it keeps the parts coherent, gives natural checkpoints, and lets sections be regenerated individually — which is also cheaper than re-running a forty-page generation to fix one chapter.

distractors.A: Streaming is a delivery mode and has no bearing on how much the model may generate. The same ceiling applies to a streamed response; it simply arrives incrementally before being truncated.
distractors.B: Sampling varies wording, not the fundamental length a forty-page guide requires. Retrying a request whose output cannot fit reproduces the truncation and pays for it each time.
distractors.D: A value above the ceiling is rejected, and ignoring a validation error means the request never runs at all. This substitutes a hard failure for a truncation without producing any output.

explanation.concept: Input and output ceilings are separate constraints, and the output ceiling cannot be raised by transport choices or retries. When a deliverable legitimately exceeds it, decompose the task — plan then sections, or chapter-at-a-time — and assemble client-side. That also converts one expensive all-or-nothing call into independently retryable units.
explanation.tip: 'Already at the maximum' plus 'the same on other models' is the stem telling you the parameter space is exhausted. Once that is stated, every option that tunes a parameter is dead and the answer must change the task shape.

topic: What jitter adds to exponential backoff
stem: In a retry policy, what does randomised jitter provide that exponential backoff on its own does not?

options.text: It shortens the total time spent retrying, because some of the waits come out randomly shorter.
It guarantees that a retry never fires before the server's advised retry-after interval has fully elapsed.
It bounds the number of attempts a client may make, so retries cannot continue indefinitely.
It decorrelates retry timing across clients, so a fleet that failed together does not retry in unison.

explanation.correct: Exponential backoff controls how hard one client pushes over time. It does nothing about the fact that a hundred clients rejected in the same instant will compute the same delays and collide again on every subsequent attempt, keeping the service pinned. Randomising each wait spreads those attempts across the interval so recovery is gradual rather than a series of synchronised waves. The larger the fleet, the more jitter matters and the less backoff alone achieves.

distractors.A: Randomisation makes individual waits shorter or longer around the schedule; it is not a speed optimisation. Any apparent gain comes from the fleet colliding less, not from any one client waiting less.
distractors.B: Honouring a server-advised interval is a separate rule that takes precedence over the computed delay. Jitter is about spreading load, and applied naively it can produce a wait shorter than the advice.
distractors.C: Bounding attempts is the job of a retry budget or a circuit breaker. Jitter changes when attempts happen, never how many there are.

explanation.concept: Backoff bounds the load one client offers; jitter decorrelates load across many. Both are needed, and neither bounds total attempts — that requires an explicit budget. In fleets that deploy identically and fail together, correlated retries are the mechanism that turns a brief limit event into a sustained outage.
explanation.tip: Backoff, jitter and retry budget solve three different problems: how hard, when, and how many. Items on this topic almost always hinge on keeping them apart.

topic: Reserving output headroom as history grows
stem: A contact-centre assistant replays the full conversation on every turn and finishes each escalation with a written summary for the case record. To keep long escalations from being rejected, the client computes the output allowance as the context window minus the current input size. Most conversations are fine, but on long escalations — exactly the ones the case record matters most for — summaries come back visibly clipped with a `max_tokens` stop reason.

options.text: Reserve an output budget sized from what the summaries need, and trim older turns to fit the input into what remains.
Drop the dynamic calculation and set the allowance to the largest value the model accepts on every request.
Start a fresh conversation once an escalation passes a 40-turn threshold, so the replayed history never grows large.
Accept the clipping and add a second call that expands the clipped summary into a complete case record.

explanation.correct: The current formula treats output as whatever is left over, so the requirement that matters least urgently — replaying every historical turn — silently outbids the requirement that matters most. Inverting the priority fixes it: decide first how much room the summary needs, protect that, and make the history fit the remainder. That turns an invisible quality failure on the longest cases into an explicit, tunable decision about how much history to carry, which is the decision the team should be making anyway.

distractors.B: A fixed maximum allowance takes no account of how much input the request already carries, so on long escalations the request is rejected outright. This trades clipped summaries for failed calls.
distractors.C: Cutting the conversation at a turn threshold discards the escalation context that the summary is supposed to capture, and long escalations are precisely where continuity matters. It solves the budget problem by destroying the product requirement.
distractors.D: A second call cannot recover content the first was never given room to write, and the model would be expanding a clipped summary rather than the conversation. It adds cost and latency to paper over the sizing error.

explanation.concept: Input and output share one window, so the budget must be allocated deliberately rather than left to whichever side grows. Reserve the output allowance first from the task's real needs, then admit as much input as the remainder allows, with an explicit trim or summarise policy for the overflow.
explanation.tip: 'Fails only on the longest cases' points at a budget that is computed rather than allocated. Ask which side of the window is being treated as the leftover — that side is where the defect is.

topic: Reducing time-to-first-token on a large-prefix request
stem: A public-records search assistant sends a 30,000-token invariant reference corpus plus a short user query on every call. Its p95 time before the first token reaches the user is 6.5 seconds, against an internal target of 2 seconds. Answers are short. Which THREE changes address that metric? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Cache the invariant corpus behind a breakpoint so it is not reprocessed from scratch on every request.
Raise the output allowance so the model is never constrained while producing an answer to a records query.
Stream the response so the first token reaches the user as produced, not after the answer is finished.
Group several users' queries into a single request so the 30,000-token corpus is amortised across them.
Move rarely-consulted portions of the corpus out of the standard request and load them only when needed.

explanation.correct: Time-to-first-token on this shape of request is dominated by processing 30,000 tokens of prefix before generation can begin, plus, without streaming, waiting for the whole answer before anything is shown. Caching removes the repeated processing of an invariant prefix; trimming the prefix reduces the work that must happen even on a miss; streaming removes the wait for completion from what the user experiences. Each attacks a distinct component of the measured 6.5 seconds.

distractors.B: The allowance governs how much may be generated, and the stem says answers are short, so it is not binding. Nothing about a larger ceiling makes the first token arrive sooner.
distractors.D: Bundling users into one request means nobody sees anything until the last query in the bundle is answered, which raises first-token time rather than lowering it. It also mixes unrelated users' queries in one context, which is a separate problem of its own.

explanation.concept: Decompose latency before optimising it. Time-to-first-token is prefix processing plus queueing plus the model's first-token work; total time adds generation. Caching and prefix reduction attack the first component; streaming changes when the user is exposed to the second. Batching and output limits target throughput and length, which are different metrics.
explanation.tip: When the metric is explicitly time-to-first-token, ignore every option about total generation. Only things that happen before the first token counts.

topic: Driving admission control from rate-limit response headers
stem: A retail media platform currently discovers it is near its throughput ceiling only when requests start being rejected. The platform team wants to shape traffic before rejections begin. They have been explicit that they will not hard-code any figure that could change when the account's limits are revised, because a stale constant caused a previous incident.

options.text: Sample the rejection rate over a rolling window and reduce client concurrency once it crosses a threshold.
Configure a fixed requests-per-second cap in the gateway, derived from last quarter's observed peak traffic level.
Drive admission control from the remaining allowance and reset time reported in the rate-limit response headers.
Route overflow requests through a second organisation account so the primary account's allowance can recover.

explanation.correct: The responses already carry the account's current allowance state, which is authoritative and moves automatically when limits are revised — exactly what a team burned by a stale constant needs. Feeding remaining allowance and reset time into an admission controller lets the platform slow down while headroom is still positive, so rejections become the exception rather than the signal. It is the only option that is both proactive and free of a hard-coded figure.

distractors.A: Reacting to the rejection rate means the rejections have already happened, which is the situation the team is trying to leave. It is a useful safety net underneath proactive shaping, not a substitute for it.
distractors.B: A constant derived from last quarter is precisely the stale figure the team ruled out, and it goes wrong in both directions: throttling below a raised limit, and overshooting a lowered one.
distractors.D: Spreading load across accounts is a commercial and governance manoeuvre rather than traffic shaping, and it leaves each account with the same blindness to its own headroom.

explanation.concept: Prefer server-reported state over client-side constants for anything the provider controls. Rate-limit headers make admission control adaptive: shape against reported remaining allowance, treat rejections and their advised retry interval as the fallback, and keep no limit figures in configuration.
explanation.tip: When a stem forbids hard-coded values, it is pointing at a source of truth that arrives with the responses. Look for the option that reads state rather than assuming it.

topic: Effect of prompt caching on model output
stem: What effect does enabling prompt caching have on the content of the model's response?

options.text: A previously produced response is returned verbatim whenever the same prompt is seen again.
None: caching changes how the prefix is processed and billed, not what the model produces for a request.
Responses become more consistent, because the cached prefix also fixes the sampling behaviour.
Responses become shorter, because content covered by the cache does not need to be restated.

explanation.correct: Prompt caching operates on the input side. It lets the prefix be reused rather than reprocessed, which reduces what the request costs and how long it takes to begin generating, and the model then generates the response in the ordinary way. Nothing about the sampled output is stored or replayed. This matters in practice because it means caching can be adopted as a pure cost and latency change with no eval impact — and equally, that it cannot be used to make behaviour more repeatable.

distractors.A: This describes response caching, an application-level pattern where a prior answer is stored and served again. It is a legitimate technique with entirely different correctness and staleness implications, and it is not what a prompt cache does.
distractors.C: Sampling is unaffected by how the prefix was processed. Teams that expect consistency from caching are usually reaching for a different mechanism, such as lower sampling temperature or a deterministic post-processing step.
distractors.D: Length is driven by the instruction and the task. Caching changes nothing the model is asked to do, so it has no reason to write less.

explanation.concept: Distinguish prompt caching from response caching. The first reuses processed input and never changes the output distribution; the second reuses an output and must be reasoned about for freshness and correctness. Only the first can be enabled without re-running your evals.
explanation.tip: If a proposal claims caching will improve consistency or shorten answers, it has confused input caching with output caching. Naming which side of the request a mechanism touches resolves most of these items.

topic: Correct statements about idempotency around a generation call
stem: A team is adding idempotency to a pipeline in which a Claude call is followed by a write to a customer record. Which TWO statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Setting sampling temperature to zero makes a retried generation return identical content, enough to deduplicate the write.
The guarantee must be enforced at the mutating step, keyed by a caller-supplied value that stays stable across retries.
Idempotency becomes unnecessary once the client's own retry logic is removed from the pipeline entirely.
A retried generation call may return different content, so deduplication cannot be based on comparing outputs.
The idempotency key should be derived by hashing the model's response, so identical outputs collapse into a single write.

explanation.correct: These two are the same principle from opposite directions. Because a regenerated response is not guaranteed to match the first, the output cannot serve as an identity for the work, which rules out any comparison-based deduplication. What is stable across retries is the business event that triggered the work, so the key must be derived from that and enforced where the state actually changes. Put together, they make the whole path safely replayable regardless of what the model returns on any given attempt.

distractors.A: Even a perfectly repeatable generation would not help: the first write has already landed, and a second identical write is still a second write. Building a data-integrity control on assumed sampling determinism is fragile in principle and unnecessary in practice.
distractors.C: Removing client retries removes one source of duplicates and leaves several others — process restarts, queue redelivery, upstream replays, and operators reissuing a request by hand. Any at-least-once path reintroduces the problem.
distractors.E: Hashing the response makes the key depend on the thing that varies, so two legitimate attempts produce two keys and two writes, while two genuinely distinct events that happen to produce identical text collapse into one. It fails in both directions.

explanation.concept: Idempotency keys must be derived from the invariant business event, never from a model output, and must be enforced at the point of mutation rather than at the point of generation. Model calls are safely repeatable; the writes that follow them are not, and that is where the guarantee belongs.
explanation.tip: Two of these five talk about the model and three about the write. The ones that try to make the model the source of identity are wrong on principle, before you reason about the specifics.

topic: Hedged requests to cut tail latency safely
stem: A live-sports product generates one-line commentary updates with a hard 900ms budget from event to display; a late line is discarded rather than shown. Median latency is 300ms but p99 is 2.4 seconds, and the tail is what viewers notice. The call is read-only and has no side effects. The team proposes issuing a second identical request whenever the first has not returned within 350ms.

options.text: Lower the client timeout to 350ms with a single retry, which achieves the same tail reduction far more simply.
Hedge every request from the outset so the faster of the two always wins, treating the extra spend as the price of the latency target.
Reject hedging outright: duplicating requests under a 900ms budget can only add load and lengthen the tail.
Adopt threshold hedging, cancel the loser when one returns, cap the hedged share of traffic, and confirm there are no side effects.

explanation.correct: Hedging is the right tool here — the work is idempotent by nature, being late is worthless, and a 350ms threshold leaves 550ms for a second attempt against a 300ms median, so the arithmetic works. The discipline is what makes it safe: cancelling the loser stops paying for generation nobody will read, capping the hedged share bounds the extra load so the mechanism cannot amplify a slowdown into an outage, and confirming the absence of side effects is what makes duplication acceptable at all.

distractors.A: Abandoning the first attempt at 350ms throws away a request that would frequently have returned at 400 or 500ms, well inside budget. Sequential retry converts a race into a restart and makes the tail worse for the very requests it targets.
distractors.B: Unconditional duplication doubles the offered load to improve a tail that only affects a small fraction of traffic, which is a poor trade against a shared throughput ceiling and can create the congestion it is meant to escape.
distractors.C: Blanket rejection ignores that this workload has exactly the properties hedging requires. The concern about added load is real, which is why hedging is capped and thresholded rather than abandoned.

explanation.concept: Hedging trades capacity for tail latency and is legitimate when the call is side-effect free, the threshold sits well above the median but far enough below the deadline to allow a second attempt, the loser is cancelled, and the hedged fraction is capped. Without those four conditions it is an amplifier rather than an optimisation.
explanation.tip: Check the arithmetic first: threshold plus median must fit inside the budget, or hedging cannot help. Then look for cancellation and a cap — an option missing either is describing an outage generator.

topic: Persisting canonical turns rather than rendered requests
stem: A telehealth triage assistant persists conversation state so patients can resume a session and clinicians can review what was exchanged. The implementation stores the fully rendered request that was sent to the API — system content, entire replayed history and all — as one blob per turn. Six months in, the team cannot say which prompt version produced a given reply, cannot replay a conversation under a revised prompt, and the store is growing quadratically because every turn re-persists the whole history.

options.text: Persist each structured turn once with the prompt and model version identifiers, and render the request at call time.
Continue storing rendered requests, but compress each blob and shorten the retention period to 90 days.
Store only the final assistant reply for each turn, since that is what clinicians actually review afterwards.
Store a hash of the rendered request alongside each reply so that prompt changes can at least be detected after the fact.

explanation.correct: The rendered request conflates three things with different lifecycles: the conversation, the prompt template, and the model choice. Splitting them fixes all three symptoms at once. Turns stored once give linear rather than quadratic growth; a recorded prompt and model version answers the provenance question directly; and because the request is rendered at call time from stored inputs, a conversation can be replayed under a new prompt to see what would have changed — which is what makes evaluation and incident review possible at all.

distractors.B: Compression and shorter retention reduce the bill while leaving the growth quadratic and the provenance question unanswered. Shorter retention actively works against a clinical review requirement.
distractors.C: Discarding what was sent makes the record unauditable: a reply is only interpretable against the context that produced it, and resume-a-session needs the patient's turns too.
distractors.D: A hash detects that something changed without saying what, and cannot be used to reconstruct or replay anything. It records the existence of a problem rather than the information needed to investigate it.

explanation.concept: Store conversation state as canonical structured turns plus the version identifiers of everything that shaped the request, and treat the rendered payload as derived. That keeps growth linear, makes provenance explicit, and lets stored conversations be re-run under new prompts or models as evaluation inputs.
explanation.tip: Quadratic growth in a per-turn store is the signature of persisting the replayed history each turn. Where a stem lists several unrelated-looking symptoms, look for the single representation choice that explains all of them.

topic: Multi-tenant prompt caching and prefix matching
stem: A SaaS vendor serving 900 corporate customers wants to cache a 12,000-token instruction and schema block that is byte-identical for every customer. Each request also carries customer-specific documents. The security review has blocked the change on the grounds that a shared cache means one customer's data could be served to another. The engineering lead needs a resolution that satisfies the reviewer without giving up the saving.

options.text: Give each of the 900 customers its own cached prefix by appending their customer identifier to the instruction block.
Accept the objection and rule prompt caching out for any workload that serves more than one corporate tenant.
Keep the invariant instruction and schema in the shared prefix and place customer documents after the breakpoint.
Encrypt the customer documents before including them so no readable customer data can ever enter the cache.

explanation.correct: A cache entry is keyed by the prefix itself, so a request can only match content it has already supplied — the mechanism returns processing savings, not content. The shared block here is the vendor's own instructions and schema, containing no customer data at all, while customer documents sit after the breakpoint and are never part of a shared entry. That structure is what makes the reviewer's concern concretely unreachable, and it is also the arrangement that maximises the saving because all 900 customers converge on one prefix.

distractors.A: Salting the prefix per customer fragments one heavily-used entry into 900 sparse ones, so most requests pay a write and collect no read. It buys no protection that prefix matching does not already provide, at the cost of the entire benefit.
distractors.B: Abandoning caching gives up a large, safe saving on content that is the vendor's own boilerplate. Blanket rules of this kind usually indicate the mechanism was not examined, which is what the resolution needs to address.
distractors.D: Content the model must read cannot be encrypted and still be useful, and the documents are outside the shared prefix in any case. This adds an unusable control against a risk that the structure has already removed.

explanation.concept: Prompt cache reuse requires an exact prefix match, so a hit is only available to a caller that already holds the identical content. Design multi-tenant prompts by placing tenant-invariant material in the shared cached prefix and all tenant data after the breakpoint — which is simultaneously the correct isolation posture and the best-performing one.
explanation.tip: When a security objection and a cost objective appear to collide, check whether the mechanism actually works the way the objection assumes. Here the two are aligned once the prefix semantics are stated plainly.

topic: Streaming as a liveness signal on long calls
stem: Setting aside how the wait feels to a user, why is streaming operationally useful for a single long-running generation?

options.text: It gives the client continuous evidence of progress, so a stall can be told apart from slow generation.
It reduces the total number of tokens the model must generate to satisfy the same long instruction.
It removes the response from the account's throughput accounting for the period the stream is open.
It lets a single response exceed the model's output ceiling by delivering the remainder in later events.

explanation.correct: A non-streamed long call is opaque: until the body arrives, a healthy sixty-second generation and a dead socket look identical, so any timeout has to be set generously enough to cover the former and therefore too generously to catch the latter quickly. A stream turns that into an observable process. Regular events prove the work is alive, which lets the client enforce a tight timeout on the interval between events while still permitting a long total duration.

distractors.B: Generation is unaffected by how the result is delivered. The same prompt produces the same work whether the bytes arrive in one body or many.
distractors.C: Accounting follows the tokens processed and produced, not the shape of the connection. Nothing about streaming changes what a request consumes from a throughput allowance.
distractors.D: The output ceiling constrains what may be generated, not how it is transmitted. A streamed response that reaches the ceiling is truncated exactly as a non-streamed one would be.

explanation.concept: Streaming has an operational benefit independent of user experience: it converts an opaque wait into an observable one, enabling inter-event timeouts, progress metrics, and early cancellation. On long generations this is often the stronger argument for streaming, and it applies even when no human is watching.
explanation.tip: The phrase 'setting aside how the wait feels' removes the obvious answer on purpose. Reach for what streaming gives the operator: visibility, cancellability, and a better timeout.

topic: Recovering from an ambiguous batch submission
stem: A retail analytics team submits a 90,000-request batch each night. Last night the submission call failed with a network error after the request body had been sent, so the client has no confirmation of whether the batch was registered. The on-call operator must act before the morning deadline. A duplicate batch would double the night's spend and produce two result sets the loader cannot tell apart. What should the operator do next?

options.text: Resubmit immediately, since a duplicate batch is cheaper than missing the deadline; delete the surplus afterwards.
List the jobs the batch service registered around the failed submission and match one by creation time and request count; submit only if none is found.
Wait for the usual turnaround window to elapse and resubmit only if no results have appeared by then.
Resubmit under a new identifier and reconcile the two result sets against the source records in the morning.

explanation.correct: An error after the body was sent is the classic ambiguous outcome: the operation may have succeeded even though the caller never learned it did. The resolution is to ask the authoritative system what state it is in before acting: the service's own list of registered jobs settles whether last night's submission landed, and creation time, request count and the per-request identifiers the client supplied make the match unambiguous. Checking costs seconds, resolves the ambiguity definitively, and protects both the deadline and the spend — which is exactly why a submission should be recognisable from the service's own records.

distractors.A: This accepts the duplicate the stem says the loader cannot distinguish, so 'delete the surplus afterwards' is not an operation anyone can actually perform. It also doubles the spend on a guess.
distractors.C: Waiting out the turnaround window before learning anything consumes the slack that the deadline depends on. If the batch was never registered, the team discovers it at the worst possible moment.
distractors.D: A new identifier guarantees the duplicate rather than avoiding it, and defers reconciliation of 180,000 results to the morning of the deadline. It converts an ambiguity that is cheap to resolve into work that is expensive to undo.

explanation.concept: A failure after the request is sent means the outcome is unknown, not failed. Make every submission recognisable in the service's own records, by listing what it has registered and matching on creation time, request count and the per-request identifiers you supplied, so the ambiguity can be resolved by querying rather than by guessing, and make that check the first step of any recovery procedure.
explanation.tip: 'Failed after the body was sent' is exam shorthand for an ambiguous outcome. The answer is always to determine the true state before acting, and the lookup that makes that determination possible is the thing being tested.

topic: Design choices that bound worst-case cost and latency
stem: An architect must give the finance and reliability teams a defensible worst case — not an average — for the cost and the elapsed time of a single request to a Claude-backed endpoint. Which TWO design choices actually bound those figures? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: An output allowance sized to the task, which caps the tokens any single response can produce.
Prompt caching on the invariant prefix, which reduces what each request costs to process.
Streaming, which delivers tokens to the caller incrementally as the model produces them.
A propagated per-request deadline bounding total elapsed time across the attempt and its retries.
A larger retry budget, which raises the probability that a given request eventually succeeds.

explanation.correct: A worst case needs hard ceilings, and only these two provide one. The output allowance is the sole mechanism that makes the most expensive possible response calculable rather than open-ended — without it, a pathological generation is bounded only by the model. A propagated deadline does the same for time, and crucially it covers retries, which is where unbounded elapsed time usually hides. Together they let the architect state a defensible maximum for a single request rather than an expectation.

distractors.B: Caching improves the typical case and leaves the worst case unchanged or slightly worse, since the worst case is a miss that pays a write. It is a strong average-cost lever and no help at all in bounding a maximum.
distractors.C: Streaming affects when bytes arrive and enables cancellation; it sets no ceiling on tokens generated or on total duration. A streamed request can run just as long as a buffered one.
distractors.E: More retries raise the worst case in both dimensions — more attempts means more generated tokens and more elapsed time. It improves eventual success probability at the direct expense of the bounds being asked for.

explanation.concept: Averages are shaped by caching, tier choice and prompt size; worst cases are set only by explicit ceilings. To make a per-request maximum defensible you need a token ceiling and a deadline that includes retries, and you need to know that resilience measures such as retry budgets trade the worst case away for reliability.
explanation.tip: The word 'worst case' rules out every option that improves a typical figure. Ask of each: does this make a maximum computable, or just make the average smaller?

topic: Output allowance as a blast-radius control
stem: A games studio generates in-world dialogue lines at high volume. To be certain a line is never truncated, the team set the output allowance to the maximum the model accepts. Last week a prompt-template change caused a subset of requests to elicit long repetitive output; every affected request ran to the full allowance, and that endpoint's daily spend was several times budget before anyone noticed. Legitimate lines run 60 to 120 tokens, and the longest ever observed was 260.

options.text: Revert the template and leave the allowance at the maximum, since the template change was the actual defect.
Add a post-generation length check that discards any response longer than 300 tokens before it reaches the game.
Move the endpoint to the Batch API so runaway spend is contained inside a scheduled job rather than the live path.
Size the allowance from the observed distribution of legitimate lines, and alert on the truncation rate.

explanation.correct: A maximum allowance on a task whose real outputs are two orders of magnitude smaller leaves the blast radius of any future prompt defect unbounded — the template change was the trigger, but the missing ceiling is what made it expensive. Sizing from the observed distribution, comfortably above the 260-token maximum ever seen, costs nothing in normal operation and caps the damage from the next defect. Alerting on the truncation rate is the other half: it makes the one risk of a tighter cap measurable rather than hypothetical.

distractors.A: Reverting fixes this incident and leaves the studio equally exposed to the next one. The stem is describing a control gap, and a control gap is not closed by removing the thing that happened to find it.
distractors.B: A length check after generation discards output that has already been produced and paid for. It protects the game from bad lines and does nothing whatsoever about the spend.
distractors.C: Batch changes the transport, not the per-request output ceiling, so runaway generation costs the same there. It would also break a live-path feature to address a problem it does not solve.

explanation.concept: The output allowance is a blast-radius control as much as a sizing parameter: it is the only thing that bounds what one malformed prompt can cost. Set it from the observed distribution of legitimate outputs plus headroom, and monitor the truncation-stop-reason rate so the cap is tightened or loosened from evidence.
explanation.tip: A stem that gives you the real output distribution alongside a maximum allowance is asking about blast radius. 'The template was the bug' is the trap — the item is about what made the bug expensive.

topic: Inter-event timeout for a long-lived stream
stem: A national rail operator's disruption-summary service streams responses that legitimately run past a minute during a major incident. The HTTP client enforces a single total-duration timeout. Set tight, it kills the long summaries produced exactly when the service matters most; set generously, genuinely hung connections hold worker threads for the whole duration and the pool exhausts during the same incidents.

options.text: Enforce a timeout on the gap between successive stream events, with a separate, generous overall deadline as a backstop.
Set the total-duration timeout to the observed p99.9 so that both the long summaries and the hung connections are covered.
Send a client-side keep-alive on the same connection to confirm the stream is still alive before continuing to wait.
Split each summary into several shorter non-streamed calls so no individual call runs past a minute.

explanation.correct: A duration-only timeout cannot distinguish the two cases because it measures the wrong thing: total time is long for a healthy summary and long for a dead socket alike. What differs is the gap between events — short and regular when generation is progressing, unbounded when the connection has hung. Enforcing on that gap detects a hang in seconds while placing no ceiling on legitimate duration, and the overall deadline still bounds the pathological case where events keep arriving forever.

distractors.B: Choosing a single generous constant is one of the two configurations already described, restated with a more precise number. Hung connections still occupy a worker until it expires, which is the failure that exhausts the pool.
distractors.C: The client cannot inject traffic into a server-to-client event stream to probe liveness; the evidence of liveness is the event flow itself, which is what an inter-event timeout observes.
distractors.D: Fragmenting a coherent incident summary into several calls multiplies round trips and reassembly work to avoid a problem that is a client timeout configuration, and it does not make any individual call's hang detectable.

explanation.concept: For streamed responses, enforce timeouts on progress rather than on duration: a short inter-event gap timeout to detect stalls, plus a generous overall deadline as a backstop. Duration-only timeouts force a choice between killing healthy long work and tolerating dead connections.
explanation.tip: When a stem describes a timeout that is wrong when tight and wrong when loose, the parameter itself is measuring the wrong quantity. Look for the option that changes what is measured.

topic: What consumes the context window in a pre-flight budget
stem: An architect is writing the pre-flight budget check for a request assembler. Which THREE of the following consume the model's context window and must therefore be included in the calculation? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: The request's HTTP headers, authentication token and correlation identifiers.
The tool definitions supplied with the request, including their JSON schemas.
The system content that carries the standing instructions and output schema.
The reserved output allowance, because generated tokens share the window with the input.
Nothing for the cached prefix, since content served from cache no longer occupies the window.

explanation.correct: Everything the model has to read occupies the window, and tool definitions are the item teams most often forget — a large tool list can consume a substantial slice before any content is added. System content obviously counts. The output allowance counts too, because input and generated output share one window, so a budget that omits the reservation will admit requests that cannot produce a full answer. Getting all three into the calculation is what makes an admission check trustworthy near the boundary.

distractors.A: Transport metadata is consumed by the HTTP layer and never reaches the model, so it has no bearing on window usage. Including it adds noise to the budget without improving its accuracy.
distractors.E: Caching changes how a prefix is processed and billed, not whether the model must read it. Cached content occupies exactly as much window as uncached content, and assuming otherwise produces an assembler that admits requests which overflow.

explanation.concept: Budget against everything the model reads or writes: tool definitions, system content, the full replayed message list, any attached documents, and a reservation for the output allowance. Caching and billing are orthogonal to window occupancy — a cheaper prefix is not a smaller one.
explanation.tip: The cached-content option is the trap in every item of this shape. Cost, latency and window occupancy are three different accounts; caching credits two of them and none of the third.

topic: Scheduling a batch workload against a hard launch date
stem: A home-goods retailer must have three million product descriptions generated before a seasonal launch in five days; nothing is customer-visible until launch. The delivery lead proposes a single Batch API submission of all three million requests, sent the day before launch so that the source catalogue data is as fresh as possible. The team has never run a batch of this size before.

options.text: Approve it: batch is the correct transport for this workload, and submitting the day before maximises freshness.
Reject batch entirely; a deadline this firm needs the realtime endpoint driven by a pool of several hundred workers.
Keep batch but submit early in tranches, track a burn-down, and hold a realtime spillover path for the remainder.
Keep batch and the single late submission, but warm a prompt cache for the shared prefix first so the job processes faster.

explanation.correct: Batch is right for the work and wrong as scheduled. Asynchronous turnaround is not a commitment the team can plan a launch against, and spending four of the five days of slack before finding out means a single unexpected outcome — slower completion than assumed, a systematic prompt defect across three million items — leaves no room to react. Tranches with a burn-down turn an opaque job into a measurable one, an early start converts slack into recovery time, and a realtime spillover path bounds the residual risk at a known cost.

distractors.A: This treats an asynchronous path as though it had a delivery guarantee, and buys marginal data freshness with the entire schedule buffer. It is also the first run at this volume, which is the worst moment to remove the margin for error.
distractors.B: Pushing three million requests through the interactive ceiling is slower and more expensive than batch, and it would contend with whatever else the account is serving. The deadline is five days away, so the batch trade is clearly available.
distractors.D: Caching reduces processing cost and does nothing to make an asynchronous turnaround predictable. It optimises a dimension the stem does not raise while leaving the schedule risk exactly where it was.

explanation.concept: When a batch workload sits behind a hard external date, treat turnaround as an estimate rather than a guarantee. Submit early, split into tranches so completion is observable, define an internal cutoff before the real one, and pre-agree a fallback path for the remainder. Slack that is not scheduled is slack you cannot use.
explanation.tip: Note when the stem says the team has never run this volume before. A first-time operation at scale should never be planned with zero recovery time, whatever the transport.
